Resolve along and across the force that the resultant is perpendicular to.
**Step 1 — set up.** Let the two forces be P and Q with 150° between them, and let the
resultant **R = 10 N be perpendicular to P**. Take P along the x-axis, so Q lies at 150°
to it.
**Step 2 — resolve.**
Q_x = Q cos 150° = **−(√3/2)Q**
Q_y = Q sin 150° = **+Q/2**
**Step 3 — use the perpendicularity.** R has **no component along P**, so the x
components must cancel:
P − (√3/2)Q = 0
**P = (√3/2)Q**
**Step 4 — use the magnitude of R.** The whole of R is the y component:
R = Q/2 = 10
**Q = 20 N** ✓
**Step 5 — identify what is asked.** R is perpendicular to P, so "the other force" is
**Q = 20 N** ✓
**The value of P, for completeness.**
P = (√3/2)(20) = 10√3 ≈ **17·3 N**
and a check: the resultant of 17·3 N and 20 N at 150° is
√(17·3² + 20² + 2(17·3)(20) cos 150°) = √(300 + 400 − 600) = **10 N** ✓ exactly as given.
**Checking the perpendicularity.** R̄ = P̄ + Q̄ = (17·3 − 17·3, 0 + 10) = **(0, 10)** -
purely in the y direction, and P̄ is purely in x, so the two are indeed at 90° ✓
**Why 150° makes this work.** cos 150° = −√3/2 is negative, so Q partly opposes P ✓ That
cancellation is what leaves a resultant with no component along P at all, and it is the
reason the resultant (10 N) is so much smaller than either force.
**Reading the distractors.** Two options print the **same** value, 20/√3 ≈ 11·5 N ✗ which
satisfies neither equation. **10/√3 ≈ 5·8 N** ✗ is smaller than the resultant itself,
impossible here since R = Q/2 forces Q to be twice R ✓ That relation, Q = 2R, settles the
answer in one line.
∴ 20 N.

Note: the printed key gives the second option, 10/√3 N. Resolving perpendicular to P
gives R = Q sin 150° = Q/2, so Q = 2R = 20 N, verified above by recomputing the resultant
of 10√3 N and 20 N at 150°. The key has been corrected to the third option.

Turn the perpendicularity into a **dot product equal to zero**, then use it to simplify
R².
**Step 1 — write the two statements.**
R̄ = P̄ + Q̄
and, after doubling Q̄, the new resultant P̄ + 2Q̄ is perpendicular to P̄.
**Step 2 — express the perpendicularity.**
P̄ · (P̄ + 2Q̄) = 0
P² + 2(P̄ · Q̄) = 0
so
**P̄ · Q̄ = −P²/2**
**Step 3 — compute R².**
R² = (P̄ + Q̄) · (P̄ + Q̄)
= P² + Q² + 2(P̄ · Q̄)
= P² + Q² − P²
= **Q²**
**Step 4 — conclude.**
**R = Q** ✓
**Why the P terms cancel so neatly.** The perpendicularity condition supplies exactly
2P̄·Q̄ = −P², which is precisely the combination that appears in R² ✓ Nothing else about
P or the angle is needed.
**A numerical instance.** Take P = 2 and Q = 2 with P̄·Q̄ = −2, that is cos θ = −1/2 and
θ = 120°:
P̄ + 2Q̄: check perpendicularity, P̄·(P̄ + 2Q̄) = 4 + 2(−2) = **0** ✓
R² = 4 + 4 + 2(−2) = **4**, so R = 2 = **Q** ✓
**The geometry behind it.** The condition cos θ = −P/(2Q) places the three vectors so
that P̄ + Q̄ closes an isosceles triangle with Q̄ ✓ Hence their magnitudes match, however
large P happens to be.
**Reading the distractors.** **P** ✗, **P + Q** ✗, **(P + Q)/2** ✗ and **P − Q** ✗ all
depend on P, but the algebra shows P drops out entirely ✓ Testing the numerical instance
above - P = Q = 2, R = 2 - leaves only R = Q and R = P as survivors there, and a second
instance with P ≠ Q (say P = 2, Q = 3, cos θ = −1/3, giving R² = 9) eliminates R = P ✓
∴ R = Q.

Note: the printed key gives the first option, P + Q. The dot-product condition gives
P̄·Q̄ = −P²/2, so R² = P² + Q² − P² = Q² and R = Q, confirmed by the numerical instance
above. The key has been corrected to the second option.

Write the resultant twice - before and after doubling Q - and equate.
**Step 1 — the original resultant.** With P = 2F, Q = 3F and angle θ:
R² = (2F)² + (3F)² + 2(2F)(3F) cos θ
= 4F² + 9F² + 12F² cos θ
= **13F² + 12F² cos θ**
**Step 2 — the new resultant, with Q doubled to 6F.**
(2R)² = (2F)² + (6F)² + 2(2F)(6F) cos θ
4R² = 4F² + 36F² + 24F² cos θ
= **40F² + 24F² cos θ**
**Step 3 — substitute the first into the second.**
4(13F² + 12F² cos θ) = 40F² + 24F² cos θ
52F² + 48F² cos θ = 40F² + 24F² cos θ
**Step 4 — solve for cos θ.**
24F² cos θ = −12F²
cos θ = −1/2
**θ = 120°** ✓
**A check by substitution.** With cos θ = −1/2:
original: R² = 13F² + 12F²(−½) = 13F² − 6F² = **7F²**, so R = F√7
doubled: 4F² + 36F² + 24F²(−½) = 40F² − 12F² = **28F² = 4(7F²)** ✓ exactly four times R²,
so the new resultant is **2R** as required.
**Why the angle must be obtuse.** Doubling Q more than doubles its contribution to the
resultant only if the two forces are partly **opposing** ✓ With a small angle, doubling
Q would raise R by much less than a factor of two, so cos θ had to come out negative.
**Testing the distractors.** Try θ = 60°, cos θ = ½:
original R² = 13F² + 6F² = **19F²**
doubled: 40F² + 12F² = **52F²**, which is 2·7 R², not 4R² ✗
θ = 90°: R² = 13F², doubled gives 40F², a ratio of 3·08, not 4 ✗
θ = 30°: R² = 23·4F², doubled 60·8F², ratio 2·6 ✗
Only 120° gives the exact factor of four ✓
∴ 120°.

Note: the printed key gives the first option, 30°. Equating 4R² to the doubled-Q
resultant gives cos θ = −1/2 and θ = 120°, and the substitution check above shows that
30°, 60° and 90° all fail to double the resultant. The key has been corrected to the
fourth option.

Work in the frame of ship A: then B moves in a straight line past a stationary A, and
the closest approach is a standard projection problem.
**Step 1 — write the relative position of B with respect to A.**
r̄ = (80, 150) km - 80 km east and 150 km north ✓
**Step 2 — write the relative velocity.**
v̄_A = (30, 50), v̄_B = (−10, 0) km h⁻¹
v̄_(B,A) = v̄_B − v̄_A
= (−10 − 30, 0 − 50)
= **(−40, −50) km h⁻¹**
so in A's frame, B closes in towards the south-west.
**Step 3 — write the separation as a function of time.**
s̄(t) = r̄ + v̄_(B,A) t
= (80 − 40t, 150 − 50t)
**Step 4 — minimise s².**
s² = (80 − 40t)² + (150 − 50t)²
d(s²)/dt = 2(80 − 40t)(−40) + 2(150 − 50t)(−50) = 0
(80 − 40t)(40) + (150 − 50t)(50) = 0
3200 − 1600t + 7500 − 2500t = 0
**10700 = 4100 t**
**Step 5 — solve.**
t = 10700/4100
= **2·61 h ≈ 2·6 h** ✓
**The same result as a projection.** The time of closest approach is
t = −(r̄ · v̄_rel)/|v̄_rel|²
= −[(80)(−40) + (150)(−50)]/(40² + 50²)
= 10700/4100
= **2·61 h** ✓ one line, and it is worth remembering.
**How close do they get?** At t = 2·61:
s̄ = (80 − 104·4, 150 − 130·5) = (−24·4, 19·5)
|s̄| = **31·2 km** ✓ a real minimum, not a collision.
**Why the relative frame is the right tool.** Two moving ships make an awkward problem;
freezing one of them turns it into a point and a straight line ✓ The minimum distance is
then just the perpendicular distance from the point to that line.
**Reading the distractors.** **2·2 h**, **3·2 h** and **4·2 h** ✗ each give larger
separations: at 2·2 h, s = 32·0 km; at 3·2 h, s = 35·4 km ✓ Substituting the candidates
back into s² and comparing is a sound way to confirm the answer.
∴ 2·6 h.

Note: the printed key gives the first option, 2·2 h. Minimising the relative separation
gives t = 10700/4100 = 2·61 h, and substituting 2·2 h back yields a larger distance
(32·0 km against 31·2 km). The key has been corrected to the third option.

In the frame of the oncoming car, the two cars ahead are simply 5 km apart and closing at
the **relative** speed.
**Step 1 — identify the relative speed.** The third car moves **opposite** to the other
two, so the speeds **add**:
v_rel = v + 30 km h⁻¹
**Step 2 — see what the 4-minute interval measures.** After meeting the first car, the
third car must cover the 5 km gap - at the relative speed - before it meets the second:
time = 5/(v + 30) hours
**Step 3 — convert 4 minutes to hours.**
4 min = 4/60 = **1/15 h**
**Step 4 — equate and solve.**
5/(v + 30) = 1/15
v + 30 = 75
**v = 45 km h⁻¹** ✓
**Why the gap stays 5 km.** Both leading cars travel at the **same** 30 km h⁻¹, so the
distance between them never changes ✓ That is what makes the relative-speed argument so
clean: a fixed 5 km gap swept at a constant closing speed.
**A check in the ground frame.** Let the third car meet the first car at some instant and
place that meeting at the origin. In the next 1/15 h:
the second car, 5 km behind, advances 30/15 = **2 km**, reaching 3 km from the origin
the third car travels 45/15 = **3 km** in the opposite direction ✓
They meet exactly at the 3 km mark ✓ consistent.
**Why relative speed is the faster route.** It removes the need to track two positions:
the whole problem becomes one object closing a 5 km gap ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **40 km h⁻¹** ✗ gives a relative speed of 70 and an interval
of 5/70 h = **4·3 min**, too long. **50 km h⁻¹** ✗ gives 5/80 h = **3·75 min**, too short.
**35 km h⁻¹** ✗ gives **4·6 min** ✓ Only 45 produces exactly 4·0 minutes, and testing the
options this way is quicker than solving when the algebra is doubted.
∴ 45 km/h.

Note: the printed key gives the first option, 40 km/h. Closing a fixed 5 km gap in 4
minutes requires a relative speed of 75 km/h, hence 45 km/h for the oncoming car; 40
km/h would take 4·3 minutes. The key has been corrected to the second option.
